name: Jacob Thompson
headline: 22-year-old certified nursing assistant in Cleveland
description:
Jacob Thompson — Jake, to everyone who knows him — moves through the memory care unit in a rhythm that looks patient but is actually a kind of held breath. His scrubs are always slightly wrinkled, the cuffs of his white sneakers gray from the linoleum. He’s twenty-two, but the bags under his eyes and the way he rolls his shoulders after every shift make him look older. On the unit, he’s the one who queues up Born in the U.S.A. on the portable speaker during afternoon activities, watching the residents’ faces shift from blank to briefly alive when the synthesizer intro hits. He knows which ones hum along, which ones tap their fingers, and which ones just stare at the ceiling. He doesn’t play the whole album — just the first three tracks, then switches to something quieter, because he’s learned that too much stimulation can tip them into agitation.

Jake’s restlessness is a physical thing. He drums his fingers on the med cart, taps his foot during meal breaks, and has already filled out three applications for travel nursing contracts in Anchorage, Fairbanks, and Nome. The brochures are folded in his locker, under a spare pair of gloves. He tells himself Alaska is about the wilderness, about needing a real challenge, but he also knows it’s about distance — from the memory care unit, from his parents’ disappointment, from the business school he left after one semester. His father, a mechanical engineer, still says “when you go back for your degree” as if dropping out was a temporary glitch. His mother, a nurse practitioner, was the one who suggested CNA training, and he’s grateful for that, but he also feels the weight of her quiet hope that he’ll eventually settle into something stable.

He grew up in a suburb of Indianapolis, comfortably middle class, with a childhood of soccer practice and summer camps and a college fund that’s now mostly untouched. The culture of his family was one of practical achievement: you get the degree, you get the job, you get the house. Jake’s own values are a tangle of that same pragmatism and a new, half-formed belief that meaning comes from showing up for people who are falling apart. He hates the way he feels when he leaves a resident’s room right after a death — hollow, useless — but he also hates the idea of doing anything else. The tension between wanting to stay and wanting to run is what keeps him moving, keeps him applying to jobs in places where the nearest hospital is a hundred miles from anything.

His personal history that still matters: the night in his sophomore year of college when he sat in his dorm room, staring at a spreadsheet for a marketing project, and felt a physical revulsion so strong he closed the laptop and didn’t open it again. He called his mother at 2 a.m., crying, and she drove three hours to pick him up. That moment — the shame of needing rescue, the relief of being taken away — is still the shape of his decision-making. He doesn’t want to need rescue again. He wants to be the one who rescues, no matter how far he has to go.
